## Introduction

In health economic evaluations such as cost-effectiveness analyses, estimating the long-term health benefits of innovative treatments over a lifetime horizon is essential. However, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) typically have short follow-up periods. Therefore, following health technology assessment (HTA) guidelines, it is important to extrapolate survival data in a statistically robust and clinically justified manner to predict life expectancy for both new treatments and standard care.

This R notebook provides a reusable, HTA-oriented framework showing analysts not only how to fit survival models in R, but how to evaluate, compare, interpret, and defend the model selected for economic evaluation.

## Defensible workflow and R tools

### NICE-recommended survival extrapolation workflow

NICE TSD14 recommends a structured four-step procedure to ensure that survival extrapolations are both statistically sound and clinically credible.

Each step builds on the last, guiding the analyst from exploratory data inspection through to a fully justified model selection that can withstand scrutiny in a health technology appraisal.

**Step 1 — Assess model assumptions & hazard structure**

Examine the observed data with graphical and statistical tools to understand which survival and hazard shapes are plausible before selecting a model.

**Step 2 — Fit candidate models**

Fit the full standard parametric family (Exponential, Weibull, Gompertz, Log-normal, Log-logistic, Generalized Gamma) and flexible alternatives where justified.

**Step 3 — Evaluate statistical fit & graphical diagnostics**

Compare fitted curves against the Kaplan-Meier estimate using AIC/BIC and residual diagnostics. Visually inspect hazard plots, probability plots, and residual plots to detect systematic departures.

**Step 4 — Evaluate external validity & decision uncertainty**

Assess whether the extrapolated curves are clinically plausible, consistent with external evidence, and robust to alternative model choices.

### R packages

Three credible specialized R packages were used to implement the workflow,

* `survival`: Fit Kaplan-Meier curves and visualizations (eg., cumulative hazard plot)
* `flexsurv`: Fit parametric and flexible survival models, residual diagnosis, and visualizations
* `GofCens`: Assess goodness-of-fit and visualizations


```{r packages}

# Install required packages
required_pkgs <- c("survival", "flexsurv", "GofCens")

for (pkg in required_pkgs) {
    if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
        install.packages(pkg)
}
}

```


```{r}

# Load required packages

invisible(lapply(required_pkgs, library, character.only = TRUE))

```

# User setting

```{r}

# Input files
control_file <- "IPD_ctrl_gp.csv"
treatment_file <- "IPD_treat_gp.csv"


# Variables definition
time_var <- "time"
status_var <- "status"
treat_var <- "treat"


# Model candidate definition
candidate_model <- c(
  "exponential",
  "weibull",
  "gompertz",
  "lnorm",
  "llogis",
  "gengamma"
)

```


## Input data

The input data, censored time-to-event data (locoregional control), were digitized from an RCT study by 
[Bonner et al, 2006](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa053422), which investigated the effect of cetuximab treatment on patients with head and neck cancer.

The `IPD_ctrl_gp.csv` and `IPD_treat_gp.csv` files contain time-to-event data for the control (n=213) and treatment (n=211) arms, with follow-up duration of 50 months.

```{r input}

# Control arm
ipd_ctrl <- read.csv("IPD_ctrl_gp.csv")

# Treatment arm
ipd_trt <- read.csv("IPD_treat_gp.csv")

# Merge data sets of two arms
ipd_merged <- rbind(ipd_ctrl, ipd_trt)


```


Inspect the first rows of the combined dataset. The column

- `time` represents follow-up time in months
- `status`: 1 and 0 represent event and censored, respectively
- `treat`: 1 and 0 represent treatment and control, respectively.


```{r inpur inspect}

# Inspect first rows of the merged data set
head(ipd_merged, 15)

```


## Step 1 - Assess model assumptions & hazard structure

Use graphical and statistical tools to determine which survival and hazard shapes are plausible before selecting a model.

### Step 1.1 Log cumulative hazard plot 

A (log) cumulative hazard plot is recommended to answer key questions:

- Are proportional hazards reasonable?
- What hazard shape is supported?


```{r log-cum-hazard km}

# Fit Kaplan-Meier curves, stratified by treatment groups
surv_km <- survival::survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ treat,
  data = ipd_merged,
  type = "kaplan-meier"
)

```

To assess whether hazards are constant over time (e.g., exponential distribution), plot cumulative hazard versus time. To evaluate monotonic changes in hazard (e.g., Weibull and Gompertz distributions), plot the logarithm of cumulative hazard against the logarithm of time.


```{r log-cum-hazard plots, fig.cap="Figure 1. Log cumulative hazard plots for the control and treatment arms."}

# Plot cumulative hazard
old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) # Set up a 1x2 plotting area

plot(surv_km,
  fun = "cumhaz",
  xlab = "Time (months)",
  ylab = "Cumulative hazard",
  col = c("black", "green"),
  main = "Cumulative hazard plot"
)

legend("topleft",
  legend = c("Control", "Treatment"),
  col = c("black", "green"),
  lty = 1,
  lwd = 1,
  bty = "n"
)

# Log both axis
plot(surv_km,
  fun = "cumhaz", 
  log = "xy",
  xlab = "Log, Time (months)",
  ylab = "Log, Cumulative hazard",
  col = c("black", "green"),
  main = "Log cumulative hazard plot"
)

legend("topleft",
  legend = c("Control", "Treatment"),
  col = c("black", "green"),
  lty = 1,
  lwd = 1,
  bty = "n"
)


```
The left plot showed that cumulative hazards appeared to transition around 10-20 months, indicating the hazard is constant over the follow-up duration.

The right plot showed that cumulative hazards increased over time, suggesting the Weibull and Gompertz distribution assumptions may be reasonable.

In addition, proportional hazards are valid across the two arms in the right plot.



### Step 1.2 Overlap KM vs parametric models 

The purpose of overlapping KM curves with the chosen parametric model curves is to evaluate goodness-of-fit for various parametric survival model candidates visually.


```{r}

# Define a vector of data sets of two arms for loop iterations
data_list  <- list(
  ipd_ctrl = ipd_ctrl,
  ipd_trt = ipd_trt
)


# Define a vector of recommended parametric models for loop iterations
distr_list <- c(
  "exponential",
  "weibull",
  "gompertz",
  "lognormal",
  'loglogistic',
  "llogis"
)

```

The package `flexsurv` can fit a variety of parametric survival models effectively. The plot shows fitted and observed data for the control and treatment arms separately.

```{r}

# Create space for global axis labels
par(
  mfrow = c(2, 5),
  oma = c(4, 4, 1, 1),   # outer margins
  mar = c(3, 2, 4, 2)    # smaller margins for individual plots
)

for (data_name in names(data_list)) {

  data <- data_list[[data_name]]

  for (distr in distr_list) {

    tryCatch(
      {
        fit <- flexsurv::flexsurvreg(
          survival::Surv(time, status) ~ 1,
          data = data,
          dist = distr
        )

        plot(
          fit,
          type = "survival",
          ci = TRUE,
          main = paste(distr, "vs KM"),
          xlab = "",
          ylab = ""
        )
        
        if (distr == distr_list[1]) {

          panel_label <- if (data_name == names(data_list)[1]) {
            "(a) Control"
          } else {
            "(b) Treatment"
          }
        
          mtext(
            panel_label,
            side = 3,
            line = 3,
            adj = 0,
            font = 2,
            cex = 1
          )}
      },
      error = function(error_message) {
        warning(
          "Model failed for dataset '", data_name,
          "' with distribution '", distr, "': ",
          conditionMessage(error_message)
        )
      }
    )
  }
}

# Global axis labels
mtext(
  "Time (months)",
  side = 1,
  outer = TRUE,
  line = 2
)

mtext(
  "Survival probability",
  side = 2,
  outer = TRUE,
  line = 2
)

```

The upper and lower panels represent control and treatment arms, respectively. From visual inspection, the Gompertz, log-normal, and log-logistic models/curves appear to fit the observed trial data better than the exponential and Weibull models.

### Step 1.3 Q-Q plot for right censored data

The purpose of using Q-Q plot is to determine any specific distribution families are compatible with the observed data.


```{r, fig.show = "hold", out.width='30%', fig.width=4, fig.height=4, fig.align='center'}

for (distr in distr_list) {
  
  tryCatch(
    {
      
    GofCens::probPlot(
        ipd_ctrl$time,
        ipd_ctrl$status,
        distr = distr,
        plots = "QQ",
        mtitle = FALSE,
        ggplo = FALSE,
        prnt = FALSE
      )
      
    usr <- par("usr")
    
    text(x = usr[1] + 0.10 * (usr[2] - usr[1]),
         y = usr[4] - 0.12 * (usr[4] - usr[3]),
         labels = distr,
         adj = c(0, 1),
         font = 2,
         cex = 1)
    
    },
    error = function(error_message) {
      warning(
        "Distribution '", distr,
        "' is not available for GofCens::probPlot(): ",
        conditionMessage(error_message)
      )
    }
  )
}



```

However, `GofCens` cannot support the Gompertz distribution. Moderate deviations appeared for the exponential, Weibull, log-normal, and log-logistic distributions, especially in mid-to-late follow-up. 

### Step 1.4 Residual plot (Cox-snell)

The residual graphics can detect any systematic lack of fit in any candidate.


```{r}

par(
  mfrow = c(2, 5),
  oma = c(4, 4, 2, 1),   # outer margins
  mar = c(3, 2, 4.5, 1)    # individual plot margins
)

for (data_name in names(data_list)) {

  data <- data_list[[data_name]]

  for (distr in distr_list) {

    tryCatch(
      {
        # Fit parametric survival model
        fit <- flexsurv::flexsurvreg(
          survival::Surv(time, status) ~ 1,
          data = data,
          dist = distr
        )

        # Cox-Snell residuals
        cs <- flexsurv::coxsnell_flexsurvreg(fit)

        # Estimate cumulative hazard of residuals
        surv <- survival::survfit(
          survival::Surv(cs$est, data$status) ~ 1
        )

        # Plot
        plot(
          surv,
          fun = "cumhaz",
          main = distr,
          xlab = "",
          ylab = ""
        )

        # Ideal Cox-Snell reference line
        abline(0, 1, col = "red")
        
        if (distr == distr_list[1]) {

          panel_label <- if (data_name == names(data_list)[1]) {
            "(a) Control"
          } else {
            "(b) Treatment"
          }
        
          mtext(
            panel_label,
            side = 3,
            line = 3,
            adj = 0,
            font = 2,
            cex = 1
          )
}
      },
      error = function(error_message) {
        warning(
          "Model failed for dataset '", data_name,
          "' with distribution '", distr, "': ",
          conditionMessage(error_message)
        )
      }
    )
  }
}


# Global axis labels
mtext(
  "Cox-Snell residual",
  side = 1,
  outer = TRUE,
  line = 2
)

mtext(
  "Cumulative hazard",
  side = 2,
  outer = TRUE,
  line = 2
)





```

The red straight line represents a perfect goodness-of-fit between the model and the observed data. By comparing the black lines of individual models with specific distributional assumptions, we can see that Gompertz, log-normal, and log-logistic performed better for the Control arm, while Gompertz alone may have best fit the observed survival data in the Treatment arm among all model candidates. 

In addition, the Cox-Snell residual is a scientifically proven measure suitable for censored survival data. 


## Step 2. Fit a common parametric survival models with two arms

Fit the full standard parametric family (Exponential, Weibull, Gompertz, Log-normal, Log-logistic, Generalized Gamma) and flexible alternatives where justified.

```{r}


model_distr_list <- c(
  "exponential",
  "weibull",
  "gompertz",
  "lognormal",
  "llogis",
  "gamma"
)

fitted_models <- lapply(model_distr_list, function(distr) {
  flexsurv::flexsurvreg(
    Surv(time, status) ~ treat,
    data = ipd_merged,
    dist = distr
  )
})

names(fitted_models) <- model_distr_list

```

### Step 3.1 Evaluate AIC of fitted models 

Evaluate robustness of the fitted model using the information criteria, AIC. The smaller the AIC scores, the more robut a model fit to the observed data. 

```{r}

aic_values <- sapply(fitted_models, function(model) {
  model$AIC
})

# Create a data frame to display AIC values for each distribution
aic_df <- data.frame(
  Distribution = names(aic_values),
  AIC = aic_values
)

# Drop row name
rownames(aic_df) <- NULL

# Sort the data frame by AIC values in ascending order
aic_df <- aic_df[order(aic_df$AIC), ]

aic_df # gompertz has the lowest AIC value


```

In line with the above graphics diagnostics, Gompertz model perform the best in fitting the observed trial data, among all the six model candidates.  


### Step 3.2 Overall KM vs best fitted model 

As a complemment evaluation, we visually inspect the fitted model curves, by comparing with non-parametric Kaplan-Meier curves for Control and Treatment arms, separately. 


```{r, fig.width=14, fig.height=7, out.width='65%'}

par(mfrow = c(6, 2),
    cex.main = 2,
    cex.axis = 1.5,
    cex.lab = 1.5)


for (mod in names(fitted_models)) {

  par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

  # Control arm

  km_ctrl <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, 
  data = ipd_merged[ipd_merged$treat == 0, ])

  plot(
    km_ctrl,
    main = paste("Control arm: KM vs", mod),
    xlab = "Time",
    ylab = "Survival probability",
    lty = 1,
    col = "black",
    mark.time = FALSE
  )

  lines(
    fitted_models[[mod]],
    newdata = data.frame(treat = 0),
    type = "survival",
    ci = FALSE,
    lty = 1,
    col = "blue"
  )

  # Treatment arm

  km_trt <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, 
  data = ipd_merged[ipd_merged$treat == 1, ])

  plot(
    km_trt,
    main = paste("Treatment arm: KM vs", mod),
    xlab = "Time",
    ylab = "Survival probability",
    lty = 2,
    mark.time = FALSE,
    col = "black"
  )

  lines(
    fitted_models[[mod]],
    newdata = data.frame(treat = 1),
    type = "survival",
    ci = FALSE,
    lty = 2,
    col = "blue"
  )

  legend(
    "bottomleft",
    legend = c(
      "Control - KM",
      "Control - Fitted",
      "Treatment - KM",
      "Treatment - Fitted"
    ),
    col = c("black", "blue", "black", "blue"),
    lty = c(1, 1, 2, 2),
    lwd = 1,
    bty = "n",
    cex = 1.5
  )

}    


```

In conclusion, based on the graphical fit check, the Gompertz model provides the best fit to the observed trial data.
